title: The hemispheres: lobes, proportions and the visual pathway
description: How cortical lesions show up in language, attention, gaze, the proportions of a weakness and the visual fields, and how early injury shapes the developing hemisphere.
why: The cortex is where localization becomes least precise and also most interesting, because a lesion there can take away abilities that no lower level of the nervous system can touch.
objectives: Recognize the signs that only a cortical lesion can produce, and use them to lift a hemiparesis to the hemisphere.
Use the proportion of face, arm and leg weakness to separate lateral cortex, medial cortex and internal capsule.
Map a visual field defect to its site, and test the fields in a child.
Separate acquired from developmental language problems, and recognize the exam patterns of perinatal brain injury.

sections.title: Signs of a cortical lesion
sections.content:
In the cord and the brainstem you localize by wiring, because tracts cross at known levels and nuclei sit beside them. The hemispheres call for different reasoning. Much of what we know about where functions live there was first learned from strokes and other lesions, true "experiments of Nature" (Brazis 2011, p. 493). At the bedside you read the map by noticing which abilities have gone missing.

**Signs that point to the cortex**

A cord or brainstem lesion can weaken a hand, but only a hemisphere lesion can take away the ability to name that hand, to notice it, or to recognize a coin placed in it. Cortical signs include these (Pearl 2014, p. 108).

- **Aphasia**, from a lesion of the language-dominant hemisphere, which is the left in almost all right-handers.
- **Homonymous visual field cuts.**
- **Cortical sensory loss**, in which touch is felt but an object goes unrecognized, two points cannot be told apart, and a number drawn on the palm cannot be read.
- **Agnosia and neglect**, classically of the left side of space after a right parietal lesion.
- **Apraxia**, in which a strong limb with normal sensation cannot carry out a complex task.
- **A dissociated weakness**, with the face and arm affected differently from the leg (next section).

Seizures and gaze preference also belong here. A **seizure** arises in the cortex, and a focal seizure is often the most precise localizing sign a child gives. A **gaze preference** comes from the frontal eye fields, each of which drives the eyes toward the opposite side. A destructive lesion lets the eyes drift toward the lesion, and a seizure drives them away (Pearl 2014, pp. 9-10).

**Hemiparesis and its neighboring signs**

When you find a hemiparesis, look for aphasia, hemisensory loss, homonymous hemianopia, unawareness of the deficit and a history of focal seizures (Brazis 2011, p. 11). Any one of them places the lesion above the brainstem, usually in the cortex or the white matter beneath it. A pure motor hemiparesis with none of them points deeper, to the internal capsule or the brainstem (Brazis 2011, p. 12).

**In a child**

Young children cannot report most of these signs, so watch for them. In a toddler neglect looks like ignoring the toys on one side, apraxia like failing to copy a simple gesture, and aphasia like losing words that were there last month.
keyPoints: Much of cortical localization was first learned from strokes and other lesions, the "experiments of Nature" (Brazis 2011, p. 493).
The signatures of a cortical lesion include aphasia, homonymous field cuts, cortical sensory loss, neglect, apraxia and a dissociated weakness (Pearl 2014, p. 108).
A destructive frontal lesion lets the eyes drift toward the lesion, and a seizure drives them away from it (Pearl 2014, pp. 9-10).
A hemiparesis with cortical signs beside it lies in the hemisphere, while a pure motor hemiparesis points deeper (Brazis 2011, pp. 11-12).

question.question: A 10-year-old wakes with weakness of his left arm and the lower half of his face. His eyes rest looking to the right, he ignores you when you stand on his left, and he does not seem troubled by the weakness. Where is the lesion?
options: Right hemisphere, involving the frontal and parietal cortex
question.explanation: Left weakness with left neglect, unawareness of the deficit and a rightward gaze preference is a right hemisphere cortical picture. A destructive right frontal eye field lesion lets the eyes drift toward it, and right parietal damage brings left neglect (Pearl 2014, pp. 9, 108). A left capsular lesion weakens the right side, and neither the pons nor the cord causes neglect.

sections.title: Reading the proportions of a weakness
sections.content:
The motor strip lies like a figure upside down over the surface of the hemisphere. The face sits low on the lateral convexity, with the arm and hand above it, and the leg folds over the top onto the medial surface between the two hemispheres. The blood supply matches, with the middle cerebral artery feeding the lateral convexity, which holds the face, arm and tongue, and the anterior cerebral artery feeding the medial surface, which holds the leg (Pearl 2014, p. 7).

**Comparing face, arm and leg**

The proportions of a weakness therefore tell you where the lesion is. Grade the face, arm and leg separately and compare them with the table (Pearl 2014, pp. 7, 9-10, 108-109; Brazis 2011, p. 11).

| Pattern | Where |
|---|---|
| Face and arm more than leg | Lateral cortex and the white matter under it: middle cerebral territory |
| Leg more than arm, face spared | Medial cortex near the top of the hemisphere: anterior cerebral territory |
| Face, arm and leg equal | Internal capsule, where the fibers are packed tightly together |

In the cortex the fibers for face, arm and leg spread over a large surface, so a lesion usually catches one part more than another. In the internal capsule the same fibers are bundled into a small space, so one small lesion can take all of them equally (Pearl 2014, p. 7).

**The face tells you the level**

Upper motor neuron facial weakness usually spares the forehead, because the upper face receives cortical input from both sides. When a lower facial droop is on the side of a hemiparesis, the lesion is generally above the upper pons, most often in the cortex, the corona radiata or the internal capsule (Brazis 2011, p. 11). If the lower face is spared and the tongue deviates toward the strong side, consider a functional weakness (Brazis 2011, p. 12).

**Tumors, seizures and children**

Tumors do not respect vascular territories, so their deficits are less tidy and build up over time (Pearl 2014, p. 10). Most childhood hemispheric lesions are not strokes, so check the proportions against the rest of the story. A focal motor seizure can show the same map in motion. Twitching that spreads from the face to the hand and then to the leg is following the order of the motor strip (Pearl 2014, p. 10).
keyPoints: The middle cerebral artery serves the face, arm and tongue, and the anterior cerebral artery serves the leg (Pearl 2014, p. 7).
Face and arm weaker than leg suggests the lateral cortex, leg weaker than arm suggests the medial cortex, and equal weakness of all three suggests the internal capsule.
Upper motor neuron facial weakness spares the forehead, and a lower facial droop on the side of a hemiparesis generally places the lesion above the upper pons (Brazis 2011, p. 11).
Tumors do not respect vascular territories, so in children proportion is a guide that needs checking (Pearl 2014, p. 10).

question.question: A 14-year-old has a weak right leg, slight clumsiness of the right hand, a normal face and normal speech. The right knee and ankle reflexes are brisk. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
options: Left medial frontal lobe near the top of the hemisphere
question.explanation: A leg much weaker than the arm, with face and speech spared, is the anterior cerebral pattern, because the leg area lies on the medial surface of the opposite hemisphere (Pearl 2014, pp. 7, 9; Brazis 2011, p. 11). A capsular lesion weakens all three equally, a lateral convexity lesion the face and arm more, and a right medial lesion the left leg.

sections.title: The visual pathway
sections.content:
The visual pathway localizes better than any other system in the hemispheres. It runs from the front of the brain to the back, and damage to each segment leaves its own pattern in the visual field, and three anatomical facts explain most of those patterns.

**Three anatomical facts**

- **The image is reversed and inverted.** The nasal retina sees the temporal field and the lower retina sees the upper field, and that inversion persists all the way back (Pearl 2014, pp. 26-27).
- **Nasal fibers cross at the chiasm.** Behind the chiasm, each hemisphere carries the opposite half of space from both eyes.
- **Behind the thalamus the fibers fan out.** Those carrying the upper field loop forward through the temporal lobe in Meyer's loop, and those carrying the lower field run through the parietal lobe (Pearl 2014, p. 27).

**Defects by site**

- Optic nerve: one eye, often with a central scotoma.
- Chiasm: both temporal fields, a bitemporal hemianopia.
- Optic tract: the opposite half-field of both eyes, a homonymous hemianopia.
- Temporal lobe: the opposite upper quadrant.
- Parietal lobe: the opposite lower quadrant.
- Occipital lobe: an opposite homonymous hemianopia, often sparing central vision (Pearl 2014, pp. 27-28).

Try each site in the figure above and watch which quadrants go dark.

**Occipital lesions**

Near the calcarine cortex the fibers from the two eyes gather into tight bundles, so a lesion there affects both eyes alike, a congruous defect. The macular area also has a dual blood supply, from the posterior and middle cerebral arteries, so a posterior cerebral infarct often spares central vision. The more congruous and the more macula-sparing the defect, the more confidently you can place the lesion in the occipital lobe (Pearl 2014, pp. 27-28).

**Testing a child**

Test each eye separately, and make sure the child's eyes stay on your face. Counting fingers in each quadrant is the best bedside method. Wiggling fingers is easier for children but less sensitive (Pearl 2014, p. 26). In younger children a small toy brought in from the side, or a blink to a threatening hand, can stand in. Presenting stimuli on both sides at once looks for extinction, a sign of neglect (Pearl 2014, p. 26). Children rarely report a field defect themselves. The first hint is often bumping into door frames on one side, or missing the start of each line when reading.
keyPoints: The retinal image is inverted and the nasal fibers cross, so behind the chiasm each hemisphere sees the opposite half of space (Pearl 2014, pp. 26-27).
A chiasmal lesion gives a bitemporal defect, a tract lesion a homonymous one, a temporal lesion the opposite upper quadrant and a parietal lesion the opposite lower quadrant.
The more congruous and macula-sparing the defect, the more likely the lesion is occipital (Pearl 2014, pp. 27-28).
Test each eye separately, prefer finger counting to finger wiggling, and present stimuli on both sides at once to look for extinction (Pearl 2014, p. 26).

question.question: A 12-year-old with headaches is found on confrontation to miss your fingers in the upper left quadrant of both eyes. The defect is roughly similar in each eye but not identical. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
options: Right temporal lobe, through Meyer's loop
question.explanation: The same quadrant in both eyes is homonymous, so the lesion lies behind the chiasm on the right. Upper-field fibers loop through the temporal lobe, so a right temporal lesion removes the upper left quadrant (Pearl 2014, p. 27). A chiasmal lesion takes both temporal fields, a left parietal lesion the lower right quadrant, and an optic nerve lesion one eye.

sections.title: Language and the developing brain
sections.content:
In the 1860s Paul Broca argued that language belongs to the left hemisphere. That overturned the old assumption that paired organs do identical work, and aphasia has stayed at the center of debates about localization ever since (Brazis 2011, p. 1). His central claim still holds in the clinic, since the left hemisphere is dominant for language in almost all right-handed people (Pearl 2014, p. 10).

:::deeper Broca's caution about lesion size
In Broca's patients, the size of the lesion in the left inferior frontal gyrus did not reliably predict how much speech was lost. A lesion of 8 to 10 mm could abolish speech, while one ten times larger only impaired it (Brazis 2011, p. 1). The map is real, but individual brains differ in how they use it, and this variation is now read as an early sign of cortical plasticity.
:::

**Testing language**

At the bedside, test language in six parts, which are fluency, comprehension, repetition, naming, reading and writing. A school-aged child can name pictures, follow a command with several steps, repeat a phrase, read a sentence and write their name. Each pattern of loss points to a different part of the left hemisphere. One well-known disconnection shows how literally the map can work. A lesion of the left visual cortex and the back of the corpus callosum leaves a patient able to write but unable to read, even what they have just written (Pearl 2014, p. 28).

**Delayed language or lost language**

With a child, ask first whether language was ever gained, and only then where the lesion is. A child whose language has always been behind most likely has a developmental language disorder, once hearing has been checked and nothing else in the story points elsewhere. That kind of delay does not localize to a focal lesion. In most people the back of the left inferior frontal gyrus is larger than the right, but this asymmetry is not found in autism or developmental language disorder (Brazis 2011, p. 493). A child who **loses** words they once had, over hours or days, has an acquired aphasia. That is a localizing sign, and it needs an urgent explanation.

**Recovery after early injury**

Children injured early in life often regain more language than adults with similar lesions, because the developing brain can reorganize. The recovery varies and is rarely complete in every respect. No published figure will fit the child in front of you, so offer the family close follow-up of their own child's progress rather than a percentage.
keyPoints: The left hemisphere is dominant for language in almost all right-handers (Pearl 2014, p. 10).
Broca saw that the size of a lesion did not predict how much speech was lost, an observation now read as evidence of cortical plasticity (Brazis 2011, p. 1).
Language that was never gained suggests a developmental disorder, whereas language that is lost is an acquired, localizing sign.
Children often recover more language than adults after early injury, but the course is variable, so avoid promising numbers.

question.question: A 5-year-old whose speech was normal for age last week now speaks in short, effortful phrases, cannot name a cup or a key, and has a slightly weak right hand. Which reading is most accurate?
options: An acquired aphasia from a left hemisphere lesion that needs urgent assessment
A developmental language disorder that can be referred for routine speech therapy
A right hemisphere lesion, since the hand weakness is on the right
question.explanation: Language that was present and is now lost, with a weak right hand, is an acquired aphasia from the left hemisphere, dominant in almost all right-handers (Pearl 2014, p. 10), and it needs urgent evaluation. A developmental disorder cannot explain speech lost since last week. A right hemisphere lesion would weaken the left hand, and selective mutism causes neither naming errors nor weakness.

sections.title: Aphasia as four switches
sections.content:
Once you know a child has lost language, ask which part has gone. The answer rests on Broca's area in the frontal lobe, Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe, and the pathway between them, which Wernicke said could cause aphasia wherever it was interrupted (Brazis 2011, p. 2).

**Four bedside tests**

Four tests do the work (Pearl 2014, pp. 18-20).

- **Fluency:** is speech effortful and sparse, or does it flow?
- **Comprehension:** can the child carry out a spoken command without copying you?
- **Repetition:** can the child say a phrase back word for word?
- **Naming:** can the child name a cup, a key, a shoe?

Each combination corresponds to a classic syndrome (Pearl 2014, p. 20, Table 2.1). Nonfluent speech with understanding preserved is **Broca** aphasia, from the dominant frontal lobe. Fluent speech with understanding lost is **Wernicke** aphasia, from the dominant temporal lobe (Pearl 2014, pp. 18-19). Losing both gives **global** aphasia, usually from a large lesion.

Repetition then splits each of these patterns in two. Preserved repetition means the lesion has spared the core language areas and lies in the cortex around them, which gives the **transcortical** motor and sensory aphasias (Pearl 2014, p. 20). Fluent speech and good understanding with failed repetition is **conduction** aphasia. Speech stays intelligible but contains sound errors, and the lesion usually lies around the supramarginal gyrus or the pathway linking the language areas (Brazis 2011, p. 524).

Naming fails in nearly every aphasia, so **anomia** alone localizes poorly (Pearl 2014, p. 20).

:::deeper Aphasia from the thalamus
When output and understanding both fail but repetition survives, the pattern is a **mixed transcortical** aphasia (Pearl 2014, p. 20). Even the dominant thalamus, a deep gray structure rather than language cortex, can cause aphasia. It is usually a mixed transcortical picture that tends to improve over weeks (Brazis 2011, p. 448; Pearl 2014, p. 20).
:::

**Using the figure**

In the figure, the child always describes the same picture, a kite stuck in a tree and a brother on a wobbling ladder, so every difference in what the child says comes from the lesion you chose.

**Conditions that mimic aphasia**

Slurred speech made of well-built sentences is **dysarthria**, a disorder of articulation rather than of language (Pearl 2014, p. 20). Neither **cerebellar mutism**, the silence that can follow removal of a cerebellar tumor, nor the speech of a confused, encephalopathic child should be read as a cortical aphasia (Pearl 2014, p. 20).

**Applying adult syndromes to children**

The four tests and their syndromes come from adult patients. A child's acquired aphasia may not sort as neatly, sit where an adult's would, or recover on an adult's schedule. Use the scheme to describe what you hear, and be cautious about predicting from it.
keyPoints: Fluency, comprehension, repetition and naming are the four bedside tests that sort the aphasias (Pearl 2014, p. 20, Table 2.1).
Preserved repetition places the lesion in the cortex around the language core, as in the transcortical aphasias (Pearl 2014, p. 20).

Fluent speech and good understanding with failed repetition is conduction aphasia (Brazis 2011, p. 524), and a dominant thalamic lesion gives a mixed transcortical picture that improves over weeks (Brazis 2011, p. 448).
Anomia on its own is relatively nonlocalizing (Pearl 2014, p. 20).
Dysarthria, cerebellar mutism after posterior fossa surgery and encephalopathy can all imitate aphasia (Pearl 2014, p. 20).

question.question: A 12-year-old is recovering from a left hemisphere injury. She talks in full sentences at a normal rate and carries out three-step commands. Asked to repeat "the ladder wobbles", she says "the lather... the ladder wobbers" and gives up. Naming is patchy, with sound errors. How do you classify her language, and what does it suggest about the lesion?
options: Broca aphasia, from the dominant inferior frontal lobe
Conduction aphasia, from a lesion around the supramarginal gyrus or the connection between the language areas
Transcortical sensory aphasia, from the cortex around Wernicke's area
Anomic aphasia, which does not localize
question.explanation: Fluent speech and intact comprehension with failed repetition and sound errors is conduction aphasia, tied to lesions around the supramarginal gyrus or the pathway linking the language areas (Brazis 2011, p. 524; Pearl 2014, p. 20). Broca aphasia is nonfluent. Transcortical sensory aphasia loses understanding and keeps repetition. Anomic aphasia requires intact repetition, and repetition is the test that localizes here.

sections.title: Perinatal brain injury
sections.content:
In the nineteenth century both William Little and Sigmund Freud wrote on the origins of cerebral palsy ([George 1992](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11618412/)). Cerebral palsy is a lasting disorder of movement and posture caused by injury to the developing brain, before or around birth or in early infancy. Two patterns of early injury are common enough that every child neurologist should recognize them from the examination alone. In both, the shape of the deficit reflects where the injury fell.

**Early hand preference and perinatal stroke**

A stroke around the time of birth often goes unnoticed in the newborn period, and the first sign may be a baby who reaches with only one hand. Hand preference before the first birthday is abnormal and points to weakness of the other hand, because true handedness develops only after twelve months ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/home_exam.html)). The child later shows a hemiplegia, with the arm and hand more affected than the leg, a fisted hand, and a leg that circumducts when walking (DeMyer, p. 340). Those are the proportions of the lateral cortex and the middle cerebral territory.

**Spastic diplegia after premature birth**

The premature brain is vulnerable in a different place. Its characteristic injury is periventricular leukomalacia, damage to the white matter around the lateral ventricles, often with injury to neurons and axons as well ([Volpe 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19081519/)). The fibers for the legs pass closest to the ventricles on their way down from the medial cortex, so they are caught first. The result is spastic diplegia, with severe spasticity in the legs, little in the arms, and little or no trouble with speech or swallowing. Double hemiplegia is the reverse, with the arms weaker than the legs and with pseudobulbar palsy (DeMyer, p. 340). Children with spastic diplegia walk on their toes, scissor their legs or walk in a crouch.

**Deep gray matter injury**

Injury to the basal ganglia and thalamus around birth, classically from hypoxia, produces a third pattern, in which slow writhing movements are mixed with spasticity (DeMyer, p. 340). Its anatomy is covered with the [[m08-loops|loops]] in Module 8.

**At the bedside**

When an infant shows an early hand preference, examine the neglected hand for tone, reflexes and fisting, and ask about the pregnancy and delivery. When a child born early walks on the toes with stiff legs and good hands, the history and the proportions point to the periventricular white matter before any imaging does.
keyPoints: Hand preference before the first birthday is abnormal and points to weakness of the other hand (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam).
Hemiplegic cerebral palsy after perinatal stroke affects the arm more than the leg, with a fisted hand and a circumducting leg (DeMyer, p. 340).
Periventricular leukomalacia is the characteristic white-matter injury of prematurity (Volpe 2009).
Spastic diplegia affects the legs much more than the arms and spares speech and swallowing, whereas in double hemiplegia the arms are weaker than the legs (DeMyer, p. 340).

question.question: A 7-month-old reaches for every toy with the left hand. The right hand is often fisted with the thumb tucked in, and the right arm reflexes are brisker than the left. The pregnancy and birth were uneventful at term. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Early left-handedness, which is normal at this age
Spastic diplegia from periventricular white-matter injury
A right brachial plexus injury from delivery
Right hemiparesis from a left hemisphere injury around the time of birth
question.explanation: Hand preference before the first birthday points to weakness of the other hand (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam). A fisted right hand with brisk reflexes is an upper motor neuron sign from the left hemisphere, and at term it fits a perinatal stroke. Handedness is not established this early, spastic diplegia affects the legs after prematurity (Volpe 2009), and a plexus injury gives a floppy arm.

quiz.question: A 13-year-old has a left homonymous hemianopia that is identical in the two eyes and spares central vision. Where is the lesion?
quiz.explanation: A homonymous defect lies behind the chiasm in the opposite hemisphere, here the right. A congruous defect that spares central vision points to the occipital lobe, where the two eyes' fibers have come together and the macula has a dual blood supply (Pearl 2014, pp. 27-28). A tract lesion is less congruous and spares no macula, and a left occipital lesion takes the right field.

quiz.question: An 11-year-old has a 30-second episode in which her head and eyes turn forcefully to the left and her left arm jerks. Afterwards she is drowsy. Where does the seizure most likely begin?
quiz.explanation: Each frontal eye field drives the eyes toward the opposite side, and a seizure excites it, so a right frontal seizure turns the eyes to the left (Pearl 2014, p. 9). The jerking left arm also points to the right motor strip. A left frontal focus would drive the eyes to the right. Seizures arise in the cortex, so a brainstem origin does not fit.

quiz.question: A 9-year-old has weakness of the right face, arm and leg to the same degree, with no aphasia, no sensory loss and normal visual fields. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
quiz.explanation: Equal weakness of face, arm and leg with no cortical signs points to the internal capsule, where one small lesion takes the bundled fibers together (Pearl 2014, pp. 7, 109; Brazis 2011, p. 12). A lateral convexity lesion weakens face and arm more, often with aphasia on the left. A medial frontal lesion weakens the leg more, and a right capsular lesion the left side.

quiz.question: A boy born at 28 weeks is now 3. He walks on his toes with stiff, scissoring legs and brisk leg reflexes, but his hands are skillful and his speech is normal for age. What best explains this pattern?
quiz.explanation: Spastic legs with relatively spared arms and normal speech make up spastic diplegia (DeMyer, p. 340). After very premature birth the characteristic cause is periventricular leukomalacia ([Volpe 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19081519/)), which catches the leg fibers first. A middle cerebral stroke affects one side, the arm more than the leg. A cerebellar malformation causes ataxia, and a neuropathy reduces the reflexes.

quiz.question: A 6-year-old has stopped speaking since removal of a tumor from her cerebellum. She watches faces, carries out simple commands, and moves both arms and legs equally. A trainee writes "global aphasia, ?left hemisphere stroke". How should her silence be framed?
options: Global aphasia from a new left hemisphere stroke, which needs imaging of the left middle cerebral territory before anything else
Selective mutism from the stress of the operation
Broca aphasia, because she is not fluent
Cerebellar mutism, a communication disorder that follows posterior fossa surgery and should not be read as a cortical aphasia
quiz.explanation: Cerebellar mutism after posterior fossa surgery should not be confused with the cerebral aphasias (Pearl 2014, p. 20). Her operation was below the tentorium, and a child who understands commands and moves all four limbs equally shows no sign of a large dominant-hemisphere lesion. Global aphasia would take comprehension and usually bring right-sided weakness. Selective mutism is silence in some settings only.

opener.parable: The cortex is where localization becomes least precise and most interesting. A lesion there can take away a word, half of the visual world, or a person's awareness that anything is missing at all.
opener.history: In 1865 Paul Broca (1824–1880) wrote that we speak with the left hemisphere, and noticed that a small lesion could abolish speech while a much larger one only impaired it. Nine years later Carl Wernicke (1848–1905) placed the understanding of words in the temporal lobe.
